The percentage tax gap is the tax gap pound value as a proportion of theoretical liability, where theoretical liability is defined as the tax gap plus the amount of tax actually received.
All excise tax gap point estimates and percentage tax gaps include duty only.
Figures may not sum due to rounding.
Ghosts are individuals who do not declare any of their income to HMRC, be it earned or unearned.
Moonlighters are individuals who are employees in their legitimate occupation but do not declare earnings from other sources of income.
Figures for previous years have been revised following methodological improvements and incorporating more up-to-date data, notably from the Office for National Statistics on consumer expenditure.
VAT receipts are expressed net of payments and repayments.

From 2019 to 2020 through to 2022 to 2023, the VAT receipts figures used to estimate the VAT gap have been adjusted to account for the impact of the VAT deferred between March 2020 and June 2020 under the ‘VAT Payments Deferral Scheme’ and the ‘VAT Deferral New Payment Scheme’ – key fiscal support measures in the government’s response to COVID-19. When estimating the VAT gap for these years, this adjustment ensures that only the net VAT receipts which related to the theoretical VAT liability in the year are properly taken into account.

The VAT total theoretical liability is the amount of VAT that should be paid in theory. This is calcualted by applying the rate of VAT on expenditure where VAT should be payable, assuming that there is no fraud, avoidance, or losses due to error or non-compliance.
The VAT total theoretical liability includes irrecoverable VAT, which is the VAT paid on ‘finally taxed expenditure’ which cannot be reclaimed, for example by those not registered for VAT.
Tobacco includes hand-rolling tobacco and cigarettes.
The beer estimate for 2005 to 2006 and 2006 to 2007 is based on the beer upper bound estimate. All other years are based on the central estimate.
The hydrocarbon oils estimate for years following 2016 to 2017 are not directly comparable to previous years due to a methodological change.
Lower estimates have been projected from 2016 to 2017 onwards.
The tax gap includes both duty and VAT.
Figures for the tax year 2020 to 2021, 2021 to 2022, 2022 to 2023, 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025 have been projected from 2019 to 2020.
Negative numbers have been truncated at zero.
The upper (or lower) bounds for both cigarette and hand-rolling tobacco cannot be combined. Only the central estimates are simultaneously possible.
The cigarettes illicit market figures are based on weighted average price (WAP) data for all UK duty paid cigarettes.

Figures for the tax year 2020 to 2021, 2021 to 2022, and 2022 to 2023 have been imputed based on known values from 2019 to 2020 and 2023 to 2024. Figures for the tax year 2024 to 2025 have been estimated based on established historical trends.
The weighted average price (WAP) data for all UK duty paid hand-rolling tobacco is not available prior to tax year 2012 to 2013, so the losses are based on the price of a ‘typical brand’.
Tax gap figures for tax years 2014 to 2015 and 2015 to 2016 are rolled forward from 2013 to 2014.
Tax gap figures from 2016 to 2017 are not directly comparable to previous years due to a methodological change.

The rate of non-compliance in the tax year 2016 to 2017 is used for estimate in 2017 to 2018 and 2018 to 2019. The rate from 2019 to 2020 is used again for 2020 to 2021 and 2021 to 2022. The rate from 2022 to 2023 is also used for 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025.
Market share figures are limited to values between 0% and 100%
Consumption estimates are based on the weighted average price (WAP) of cigarettes.
Consumption estimates are based on the 'typical brand'. Weighted average price (WAP) data for hand rolling tobacco is not available prior to 2012 to 2013.
Tax gap estimates from 2023 to 2024 are projected based on Self Assessment liabilities figures for the respective years and will be revised when operational data becomes available.
Compliance yield for 2020 to 2021 and 2021 to 2022 is based on recorded yield for 2019 to 2020. Compliance yield for all other years is based on period of settlement of enquiry.
The non-payment figure for 2020 to 2021 and 2021 to 2022 is the total non-payment for these years split equally between them.
Liability refers to the actual amount expected to be received by HMRC based on taxpayer declarations and HMRC's compliance activity.
The PAYE employer compliance tax gap is made up of 3 components: small businesses, mid-sized businesses and large businesses
Compliance yield is recoded by period of settlement of enquiry.
Year relates to when the enquiry was opened, as employer compliance queries are not made in relation to an annual return.
Values exclude the tax gap relating to avoidance; this figure is available at an aggregate level for Income Tax, NICs and Capital Gains Tax.
Projection factor applied to the gross tax gap estimate for 2022 to 2023 to produce projected estimates from 2023 to 2024 onward. This is based on the trend in estimated PAYE liabilities.
Compliance yield is the total yield from closed risks, plus the estimated compliance yield from open risks.

A projection factor is applied to the compliance yield estimate for 2022 to 2023 to produce projected estimates from 2023 to 2024 onward. This is based on the trend in estimated PAYE liabilities.
The tax gap estimates are projected in 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025 by applying uplifts to the underlying user numbers based on previous years.
